newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: TENNIS-HINGIS SETS SIGHTS ON NUMBER ONE SPOT.
newsitem.headline: TENNIS-HINGIS SETS SIGHTS ON NUMBER ONE SPOT.

text.p: Martina Hingis has broken so many records in her young life that on Saturday, at the tender age of 16 years and three months, she found there was only one more to aim at -- becoming the youngest ever world number one.
The Swiss prodigy spoke of her goal after becoming the game's youngest ever Grand Slam champion by squashing France's Mary Pierce 6-2 6-2 in the Australian Open final.
"Just an injury could hold me away from that right now," said the new world number two, wearing the cheeky grin which has so annoyed her hapless opponents in this tournament.
"I have a pretty big chance," she added.

"I just want to play very good tennis at the next tournmanet and see what happens in Paris (at the French Open) and the other Grand Slams. Maybe there is a little step to get better and better and just try to make number one."
How did she feel to be the youngest Grand Slam singles winner in the history of professional tennis?
"It's just another record for me," Hingis shrugged. "I've had so many records already."

Hingis breaks records like other players snap racquet strings: at age 12 the youngest ever Grand Slam junior champion, at 15 the youngest Grand Slam winner in the doubles at Wimbledon last year, at 16 the youngest to win $1 million in a season.

She took only a few weeks to realise her New Year's wish to win a Grand Slam title this year and may not need much longer to claim the number one spot from Germany's Steffi Graf, who lost out in the fourth round in Melbourne.
Hingis, who earned 739 ranking points at Melbourne Park, still trails Graf by about 900 points. Good results on the tour and another Grand Slam could breach the gap.
So far, the youngest player to earn the top women's ranking is Monica Seles who shot to world number one in 1991 at the age of 17 years, three months, nine days. Hingis is a year younger.
On Friday Hingis became the Australian Open's youngest ever title-holder when she and Belarussian Natasha Zvereva won the women's doubles in another one-sided victory.
"Next year I'm going to try to win the mixed doubles and win all of them," Hingis joked to the packed Centre Court crowd on Saturday after lifting her second cup of the tournament.
She has proven to be as cheeky and playful off the court as she is on it, joking sarcastically to reporters that her first Grand Slam victory meant "nothing at all. Just another title".
The way she hugged her mother and coach, Melanie, on Centre Court after the match told a different story. Both had clearly dreamed of the moment.
"I think we are a great team," Hingis said. "In this tournament we were just better than everybody else."
Born in Czechoslovakia and raised in Switzerland, Hingis stops giggling when asked if she can emulate the feats of Czech tennis great Martina Navratilova.
Her mother, a former Czechoslovak champion herself, named Hingis after the 18-times Grand Slam singles champion who won more than 300 doubles and singles titles.
The Navratilova name is one Hingis does not take lightly.
"Oh the big one -- MN," Hingis said. "She's just been such a great athelete and she won so many Grand Slam titles, in singles, doubles and mixed....
"I've got enough time to pick her up in all these tournaments but I don't think anybody else can win so many titles as her."
